The commissioning procedure is considered critical to maintaining the integrity of the hot tank, as it can generate dangerous thermal gradients when the tank is empty or below the minimum inventory level. Exposing the tank to hazardous conditions during commissioning can cause plastic deformation in the floor and accelerate failure mechanisms such as SRC, creep, and/or LCF. Previous modeling studies under the DOE SETO-funded project, agreement DE-EE0010316, indicated the potential for buckling during commissioning with radial temperature differences around 30°C, followed by an increase in the fluid level. A review of available operational data during commissioning identified similar conditions that were considered potentially damaging (see Figure 32). 3.2 Tank Commissioning Process The commissioning process for a commercial two-tank nitrate salt storage system is complex and can take several days or weeks. The general process is summarized as follows: • Preheat to at least 20°C above the solidus temperature of the storage medium with the air preheating system. • Containment test with cold molten salt from the cold tank: This entails filling the tank to the maximum operating level (at a lower temperature than typical operations, thus higher fluid density) and holding it for some hours. • After the containment test, the level is reduced to the level appropriate for the electrical heating system. Most commercial projects are equipped with embedded heaters or a recirculating electrical heater. • The tank is heated from the preheating temperature to the maximum heating system temperature at a constant fluid level. The maximum heating system temperature is assumed to be 400°C. • Heating to temperatures higher than the heating system allows is achieved with the Receiver assembly. Multiple procedures may exist for heating with the receiver assembly depending on the specific operation and internal tank temperature measurements.
